name: Aviptadil
lead: Aviptadil is a synthetic form of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide first characterised in 1970.[1][2] It has been used as an injectable in combination with phentolamine for erectile dysfunction in some European countries, and it has been studied as an intravenous or inhaled treatment for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pulmonary hypertension and COVID-19 respiratory failure.[1][3][4]

The largest randomized test, the TESICO trial in COVID-19 respiratory failure, was published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine in 2023; a reference summary states that it showed no significant improvement in outcomes versus placebo.[5][3] Aviptadil is not approved for any lung indication in the US.
It appears in this wiki because the parent peptide, VIP, is sold as a research compound. No study of aviptadil for appearance or recovery in healthy people was found.
infobox: Approved for erectile dysfunction (with phentolamine) in some countries; investigational for lung disease in the US[1][3]

paras: In the UK and some other European countries, aviptadil combined with phentolamine has been authorised for erectile dysfunction, at a much lower dose than used in lung studies.[1] A review of intracavernosal injectables includes it among agents used for this purpose.[6]

In pulmonary hypertension, a small study of single-dose inhaled aviptadil in 20 patients examined effects on haemodynamics and blood gases and safety.[7] The peptide was granted orphan designations in Europe and the US for lung conditions, according to a Grokipedia summary that should be treated with caution as an AI-generated source.[3]

Aviptadil acts on VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors. Preclinical work cited by researchers suggests it increases surfactant production, inhibits cytokine synthesis and blocks SARS-CoV-2 replication in lung cells, the rationale given for COVID-19 trials.[8][1]

A 60-day randomized controlled trial of intravenous aviptadil in critical COVID-19 respiratory failure was published in Critical Care Medicine in 2022.[8] The larger ACTIV-3b/TESICO Phase 3 trial (about 471 participants) compared aviptadil and remdesivir with placebo; its 2023 Lancet Respiratory Medicine report is the source of the finding that outcomes did not significantly improve.[5][9][3]

Inhaled aviptadil was tested in other COVID-19 trials; one Phase 2 study of 80 participants completed and others were terminated or withdrawn.[10][11][12] A 2022 case report described rapid recovery in one pregnant patient with critical COVID-19.[13]
No trials were found of aviptadil in healthy people or for cosmetic, recovery or performance purposes.

The US FDA granted fast-track designation for COVID-19 respiratory distress in June 2020, and the developer requested emergency use authorization that September; a later reference summary states the FDA declined emergency authorization.[1][3] India authorised Zuventus to market it for severe COVID-19 with ARDS in April 2022.[1]

card.summary: Synthetic VIP used for erectile dysfunction and tested in COVID-19 lung failure; no appearance evidence.
card.note: Investigational for lung disease; large COVID-19 trial reported no significant benefit.

quick.overview:
Aviptadil is a lab-made version of vasoactive intestinal peptide. In some countries it is approved, with phentolamine, as an injection for erectile dysfunction.

It was also tested for COVID-19 respiratory failure; a reference summary says the large TESICO trial showed no significant benefit. It has no studied role in appearance.
quick.mechanism: It activates VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors, producing vasodilation and anti-inflammatory effects. Preclinical work suggested effects on lung surfactant and cytokines.
quick.risks: Safety data come from patient trials in erectile dysfunction and critical illness. It is not approved for lung disease in the US, and no data exist for healthy-use contexts.
